description: No game no life, that's why we build one
summary:
Fix and Fly: Go Rocket! is a retro arcade game that lets players design, fly and evaluate a complete space mission. Players spend a limited budget on a rocket’s body, engine and interior, then fly it from Earth to repair three damaged spacecraft based on real space weather events, including the 2003 Midori-II failure and the 2022 Starlink loss. They diagnose each failure from telemetry, choose the right repair, survive an unknown solar event by buying matching upgrades, and send their findings to Mission Control.

The game addresses the challenge directly. Players design a spacecraft, manage fuel, hull health and budget, simulate the mission in flight, and evaluate the result in a report that checks each requirement. It follows NASA’s mission design process, and its radiation and heat values are based on NASA research. Every choice has a consequence, and no single build is perfect.

It matters because real missions are built from trade-offs, and space weather is a real danger for spacecraft. The game turns these ideas into something students can learn by playing, failing and trying again.
details:
WHAT DOES IT DO? 🤔

Fix and Fly: Go Rocket! is a retro arcade game that teaches players how to design a rocket that can survive space weather. Before launch, players spend a limited budget on the rocket's body, engine, and interior. Each choice has a real trade-off and real consequences. A cheap material may be light but weak against heat. A heavy shield protects the crew but costs fuel and money. There is no single perfect rocket, so players learn by trying different builds and seeing why one survives and another fails. Players are required to use creativity and long-term visionary plans to survive and accomplish the missions


WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE? 🌟

Players learn how rockets are designed and why different materials suit different jobs. They learn how space radiation, heat, and debris affect spacecraft, and how shielding works. They learn how engineers diagnose a failing spacecraft from its data and pick the right fix. They discover real stars and real cases, practices decision-making under limits, such as budget, fuel and risk. The game is simple, short, and easy to start, so it suits students with no space background.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT? 👀

We want to teach, through a simple game, how a rocket’s design, materials and choices connect to whether a mission succeeds. We hope players come away understanding that real missions are built from trade-offs, not perfect answers, and that space weather is a real risk engineers must design for. By basing the game on real NASA research and real satellite events, we want to turn curiosity about space into an understanding of how spacecraft survive.

WHAT TOOLS DO WE USE? 🦾

  • Claude (Anthropic): to refine the game design, research real events and sources, write the game code, and draft text.
  • HTML5, CSS and JavaScript (Canvas): to build the game.
  • Web Audio API: for built-in retro sound effects.
  • IbisPaint X: for our own artwork.
  • Pixabay: for background music, the warning sound, and the losing sound.
  • Google Fonts (Press Start 2P): for the retro lettering.
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages: to store the code and host the playable game.
  • Sources: NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions webinar, NASA/JPL’s Curiosity radiation results, NOAA, JAXA, IEEE Spectrum, Frontiers in Plant Science, and the other sources listed in our README.

The concept, mechanics, art, and theme are ours, and Claude helped with design, research, and code. No NASA logos or branding are used.

WHY MAKES YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE? 🎨

1. It turns knowledge into decisions.

Instead of simply presenting players with information about space, the game challenges them to apply that knowledge. Players must evaluate mission conditions, calculate risks, manage resources, and decide what action makes the most sense. Learning becomes part of the gameplay rather than something separate from it.

2. Simple mechanics, meaningful consequences.

The controls and gameplay are intentionally simple, but the decisions are not. Players have limited opportunities to make mistakes, a restricted budget, and a spacecraft hull that must be protected. Every decision has consequences, so even a small mistake can affect the entire mission.

3. It connects different space-related systems.

Space missions don't operate through isolated problems. Radiation, spacecraft integrity, fuel, power, and communication can influence one another. Our game brings these elements together, helping players understand how one problem can create a chain reaction across a mission.

4. It makes failure part of the learning experience.

Players aren't simply told the correct answer. They experience what happens when they make the wrong decision, manage resources poorly, or misunderstand a mission condition. Failure becomes feedback, encouraging them to reconsider their approach and make better decisions.

5. It puts players in the role of a mission decision-maker.

Rather than playing as someone who simply explores space, players take responsibility for keeping a mission operational. They must investigate problems, interpret information, prioritize actions, and make decisions that determine whether the mission succeeds.

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER? 💪

1. How to make the experience memorable without sacrificing education.

We wanted players to remember more than just scientific facts. The goal was to create situations where they could experience the consequences of those facts. By connecting scientific knowledge to gameplay, players have a reason to understand and remember what they learn.

2. How to translate NASA's challenge requirements into an accessible game.

Space science and mission operations can be complicated, especially for players without a technical background. We considered how to simplify these concepts into understandable mechanics without removing the important scientific and decision-making elements.

3. How to balance entertainment with educational value.

An educational game still needs to be enjoyable. We considered the difficulty, progression, resource limitations, and consequences of player decisions to make sure the experience remains engaging while still encouraging players to think critically.

4. How to make the game serve more than one purpose.

Beyond entertainment, we wanted the game to introduce players to space science, systems thinking, risk assessment, and resource management. It should be something players can enjoy while also developing a better understanding of how space missions work.

5. How to make the experience achievable and understandable within a limited scope.

Space missions involve many complex systems, but trying to simulate everything would make the game overwhelming. We had to identify which concepts were most relevant to our mission and translate them into mechanics that players could understand and interact with.
